ashwini: Born when the sun god Surya and his wife came together in the form of horses, the Ashwini twins are the physicians of the gods. As thanks for restoring youth to the aged sage Chyavana, they won the right to drink soma, the divine nectar once denied to them.
bharani: Yama was the first mortal to die, opening the road to the land of the dead and becoming its king. His sister Yami could not stop grieving, so the gods created night; as days began to turn, her tears were finally healed.
krittika: From Shiva's fiery seed, carried by the fire god Agni, a child was born and nursed by the six Krittikas, the Pleiades. Drinking with six faces, he grew into Kartikeya, the god of war who leads the army of the gods.
rohini: The moon god Chandra had 27 wives, the 27 nakshatras, but loved only Rohini. Cursed by his father-in-law Daksha, he began to waste away; saved by Shiva, the moon has waxed and waned ever since.
mrigashira: The moon god Soma is also the heavenly nectar that gives the gods their strength. When the celestial musicians, the Gandharvas, stole Soma, the Vedas tell that the gods offered Vach, goddess of speech, to win it back.
ardra: Rudra, the storm god later known as Shiva, began to cry as soon as he was born because he had no name. Each time he wept the creator gave him a name, until he held eight. The teardrop symbol is this storm's tear.
punarvasu: Aditi, mother of the gods, is the boundless sky itself. Punarvasu means "becoming good again," and Rama, the incarnation of Vishnu born as a child of Aditi's line, is said to have been born on this nakshatra's day.
pushya: Brihaspati is the teacher and priest of the gods. Whenever the gods were losing their war against the asuras, he guided them with the power of sacred prayer and turned the battle back toward victory.
ashlesha: When the gods and asuras churned the ocean for the nectar of immortality, Vasuki, king of the Naga serpents, served as the rope wound around the mountain. The coiled serpent symbol is his form, holding up that great work.
magha: The Pitris are the spirits of the ancestors. Nourished by the offerings of their descendants, they guard the family line and return blessings to the living. The throne symbol stands for the lineage and pride that are handed down.
purva-phalguni: Bhaga, god of fortune and of one's rightful share, lost both eyes after angering Shiva at Daksha's sacrifice. That is why, it is said, fortune is blind and may come to anyone.
uttara-phalguni: Aryaman is the god of promises and marriage, believed to guide the bride to her new home at a wedding. The Milky Way is called "Aryaman's path," and the ancestors are said to travel along it.
hasta: At a sacrifice, the sun god Savitar lost both his hands. The gods gave him hands of gold, and with them he now spreads his light across the sky and wakes the world each morning.
chitra: Tvashtar is the craftsman of the gods, the master who shapes every form. The Vedas say it was he who forged the vajra, the thunderbolt wielded by Indra, king of the gods.
swati: As a child, Hanuman, son of the wind god Vayu, leapt at the sun thinking it was a fruit and was struck down by Indra. In his anger Vayu stopped the wind, every creature began to suffocate, and the gods hurried to beg his forgiveness.
vishakha: Indra, god of thunder, and Agni, god of fire, are rare gods worshipped as a pair. Praised for breaking enemy strongholds together, they stand for two forces joined toward one goal.
anuradha: Mitra is the god of friendship and promises, watching over the day alongside Varuna, keeper of cosmic order. He witnesses the vows people make to each other and lends strength to those who keep their word.
jyeshtha: Indra, king of the gods, struck down the great serpent Vritra, who had dammed up the waters of the world, and set the rivers free across the earth. Jyeshtha means "the eldest," the power and responsibility of the one at the top.
mula: Nirriti is the goddess of dissolution and endings. People worshipped her to keep misfortune away, yet her power to tear the old out by the roots was also seen as the ground on which new beginnings are built.
purva-ashadha: The Apas are the water goddesses, called "the mother waters" in the Vedas. They are praised for descending from the sky to nourish the earth, washing away people's sins and impurities, and giving them new strength.
uttara-ashadha: The Vishvedevas, "all the gods," are a band of deities said to be the ten sons of Dharma, god of righteousness. Always invited to the rites for the ancestors, they are said to bring a victory that never wavers.
shravana: When the demon king Bali seized the world, Vishnu appeared as the dwarf Vamana and asked for "as much land as three steps." Granted it, he grew into a giant and with three strides measured heaven, earth and the underworld, winning the world back.
dhanishta: The eight Vasus were condemned to be born as humans for stealing the cow of the sage Vasishtha. The goddess Ganga returned seven of them to heaven at birth, and the last became Bhishma, the hero of the Mahabharata.
shatabhisha: Varuna rules the waters of heaven and the order of the cosmos, watching human deeds with the stars as his eyes. Shatabhisha means "a hundred physicians," and Varuna is believed to forgive wrongs and heal illness.
purva-bhadrapada: Aja Ekapada, "the one-footed goat," is a mysterious god seen as a form of Rudra (Shiva). Standing on one foot like a pillar holding heaven and earth apart, he is said to hold the power of storm and fire.
uttara-bhadrapada: Ahir Budhnya, "the serpent of the deep," sleeps quietly in the waters at the bottom of the cosmos. He embodies hidden wisdom and a calm strength that supports the world from below.
revati: Pushan is the god of journeys and roads, guiding lost cattle and travelers onto the right path and escorting the souls of the dead to the next world. Having lost his teeth at Daksha's sacrifice, he is offered soft porridge.
